p: The pre-solo written was three pages, stapled at the corner, in Abby's block capitals, and it sat on the folding table in the briefing room on Monday afternoon with a pencil on top of it like a paperweight.

HANGAR SIX PRE-SOLO KNOWLEDGE TEST, C172N (A. Strand). 30 QUESTIONS. OPEN BOOK: BISCUIT'S POH, YOUR SECTIONAL, THE KAPA SHEET. CLOSED BOOK: EVERYTHING ELSE.. PART 1. PARTS 61 AND 91 (WHAT YOU MAY DO ALONE, WHAT YOU MAY NOT). PART 2. KAPA (TOWER, PATTERNS, HOT SPOTS, THE SHELF). PART 3. BISCUIT (SPEEDS, LIMITS, FUEL, EMERGENCIES, THE DOOR). Show your work on anything with a number. I'll go over every one you miss before you go anywhere without me. That's not me being nice. That's 61.87.

Jordan had come straight from a shift that had ended at seven that morning, slept five hours with the blackout curtains taped at the edges, and eaten a bowl of cereal standing over the sink. She'd taken a lot of tests. Paramedic school, the national registry, recertifications every two years with a mannequin named Gary who'd been dying since 2014. She knew how she took tests. She read the whole thing first, all thirty, before she wrote a word, the way you look at the whole patient before you touch anything.

Abby didn't watch her. Abby sat at the other end of the table with her own logbook open and a calculator, adding up something with her lips moving. Every so often she wrote a number in the margin and circled it. Jordan knew what it was without asking. Twelve hundred and something. The airlines wanted fifteen hundred.

Question nine asked what Biscuit's maximum flap extended speed was, and she had to look it up, and the POH page had a coffee ring on it in the exact shape of the mug on the briefing room counter. Question fourteen asked her to draw the Class B shelves over the field with their altitudes, and she drew them without looking, and then drew a little red ring around the 80 because she couldn't help it. Question twenty two asked what she'd do if Biscuit's door popped open on rotation. She wrote: FLY THE AIRPLANE. LEAVE THE DOOR. Then she sat looking at that for a while, because it was Danny's door. He'd never fixed it. He'd said it kept him humble.
Forty one minutes. She put the pencil down on top of the pages, the way she'd found it.
Abby graded it in green without a word. Tick. Tick. Tick. A long pause on page two. Tick. Then she wrote a number at the top, circled it twice, and turned the test around.
Good, Abby said. Now the part where it counts.
Abby's Ground School: slow, steep, and alone.
What has to be true before I get out.

Sit. This is the one chapter of your training that's mostly about me signing things, so you get to watch me be careful for once. 61.87 is the regulation for student solo, and it's written as a list of things that have to be true before I'm allowed to climb out of that airplane.

First, a knowledge test. The one you just took. The FAA doesn't write it. I do, and it has to cover three things: the parts of 61 and 91 that apply to you, the airspace rules and procedures for the airport you're soloing at, and the flight characteristics and operational limitations of the make and model you're flying. So, Biscuit. When you finish, I have to go over every wrong answer with you before I can authorize the solo. Not some of them. All of them. You got three wrong, so we're having three conversations.

Second, training. 61.87(d) lists fifteen maneuvers and procedures for a single-engine airplane that you have to have received and logged before you solo, and you have to show me you can do them safely, as judged by me. Flight prep, taxi and runups, normal and crosswind takeoffs and landings, straight and level, climbs, turns, patterns, collision and wake avoidance, descents with high and low drag, flight at airspeeds from cruise down to slow flight, stalls entered from different attitudes and power settings with recovery at the first indication and from a full stall, emergencies and malfunctions, ground reference maneuvers, simulated engine failures to a landing area, slips to a landing, and go-arounds. You've done every one of those. Tomorrow I want to see slow flight, stalls, steep turns, and a ground reference maneuver again, because I'm signing that they're yours, and I'd like that to be true.

Third, the endorsements. The current FAA advisory circular for this, AC 61-65K, has sample wording, and I use it almost word for word, because words in a logbook are the only thing anybody can check later. One endorsement says you passed the pre-solo knowledge test for the 172N. One says you've received and logged the pre-solo flight training and demonstrated satisfactory proficiency and safety. One says you're proficient to make solo flights in a 172N. That last one is for a specific make and model, from the instructor who gave the training, and it's good for 90 days. 61.87(n) and (p). After 90 days I have to look at you again and sign again. It doesn't roll over because you were nice to me.

Then there's what you need with you. 61.3 says you carry your pilot certificate, which for you is the plastic student pilot certificate, and a photo ID, like your driver's license. Your medical has to be with you too. The plastic student certificate doesn't expire. Your third class medical, since you were under 40 when you got it, is good for 60 calendar months. Your logbook isn't required to be in the airplane on a local solo. 61.51 makes you carry it, with the student certificate, on solo cross-countries. Bring it anyway. If somebody from the FAA asks to see your endorsement on the ramp, you want to hand it to them instead of describing it.

How the exam asks it. Know who gives the pre-solo test (your instructor), what it covers, that incorrect answers must be reviewed before solo, that the solo endorsement is make and model specific, and that it lasts 90 days.
Solo doesn't make you a pilot. It makes you a student pilot who's allowed to be alone in the airplane. 61.89 is the list of what you still can't do, and the test likes it.

You can't carry a passenger. Not Ellie, not Claire, not Russ, who has already asked, as a joke, twice. You can't fly for compensation or hire, or carry property for hire, or fly in furtherance of a business. No international flights, except one specific route in Alaska that you'll never fly. You can't fly when the flight or surface visibility is under 3 statute miles in the day or 5 at night, and you can't fly when you can't keep visual reference to the surface. And you can't fly contrary to any limitations I write in your logbook. That's 61.89(a)(8), and it's the one that makes my handwriting a regulation.

So I'm going to write some. Day only. The KAPA pattern for now, and the practice area east when I add it. Wind, gusts, and crosswind tighter than the card you've been flying dual. Ceiling and visibility better than the legal minimum. Those aren't the FAA's numbers. They're mine, and the day they're in your logbook, they're yours too.

Two more fences. 61.93 says a student can't solo beyond 25 nautical miles from the airport, or land anywhere other than the airport you left, without more training and more endorsements. That's chapter nine. And Class B needs its own endorsement for a solo student, A.12 in the advisory circular, with training in that specific Class B. We aren't doing that. Our Class D here doesn't need a special endorsement for you. The Class B, Class C, and Class D endorsements under 61.94 are for students going for sport or recreational certificates. You're going for private. You need the tower's permission, which you already know how to get.
How the exam asks it. 61.89 is a favorite. No passengers, no hire, 3 SM day and 5 SM night visibility, visual reference to the surface, and any instructor limitations.

Now the airplane part, and first the math nobody writes on the brochure. Slow flight and stalls on the checkride have to be done from an altitude that lets you finish no lower than 1,500 feet above the ground. The ACS says it for slow flight, for power-off stalls, and for power-on stalls, and the Airplane Flying Handbook says the same thing about practicing them. Over the field that's 5,885 plus 1,500, so 7,385 MSL. The Denver Class B floor over the field is 8,000. Eight thousand minus 7,385 is 615 feet. That's the whole room. And a stall recovery is allowed to lose altitude. The ACS says right in its appendix that the examiner shouldn't demand a number for the altitude lost.

So we don't do them over the field. We go east, over Bennett, where the ground is about 5,500. Fifteen hundred above that is 7,006. Same 8,000 shelf on top. Now we've got 994 feet. I enter at 7,700, my usual three hundred under the shelf, and that leaves almost 700 feet between my entry altitude and the bottom of the box. Stalls in Biscuit lose a couple hundred feet if you're good. Plenty. Spins are a different story, and we'll get there.

The ACS doesn't print a floor for steep turns. I use the same one anyway, because the airplane doesn't know which task you're on. Ground reference maneuvers are the opposite. They're flown low on purpose, 600 to 1,000 feet above the ground, so the ground means something. Over Bennett, 6,100 to 6,500 MSL. The handbook wants at least 500 feet above any obstruction and 2,000 feet sideways from it, and it wants you away from towns, crowds, and livestock. Out east that means picking a field without cows in it, which is harder than it sounds.

Every maneuver starts with clearing turns. Two 90 degree turns, one each way, looking left, right, above, and below. High wing means the airplane above you is invisible until you lift a wing to look for it. Say the altitude out loud before you start. You know why.
How the exam asks it. Expect a scenario with a field elevation and a required AGL altitude. Add, then check what's above you. The ACS 1,500 ft AGL floor applies to slow flight and stalls.

Slow flight is flying on purpose in the place you're usually only passing through: right before a takeoff, right before a landing. The handbook's definition is good: an airspeed where any further increase in angle of attack, any increase in load factor, or any reduction in power would give you a stall warning. In Biscuit, the stall warning is the horn, the little reed whistle in the left wing root, which sounds like a kazoo with a grudge.

The current ACS wants slow flight with no stall warning. Older standards had you flying it with the horn going, and you'll hear old pilots talk about it that way. The new standard is just above the warning: altitude within 100 feet, heading within 10 degrees, bank within 10, and airspeed plus 10, minus zero. Minus zero means not one knot slower than what you picked. The handbook suggests a target of 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall speed in that configuration, and a way to find it: slow to the horn, lower the nose a little until it quits, add power to hold altitude, and read the airspeed. That's your number.

Here's what changes when you get there. The controls go mushy, because less air is moving over them, so you need bigger inputs to get the same answer. The nose is high. The engine is working hard and the airplane wants to yaw left, so your right foot is busy. And you're on the back side of the power curve, which is the part that rewires you. Down here, if you pull back, you slow down and you sink. Pitch controls your airspeed and power controls your altitude. If you lose altitude, add power. If the horn chirps, the nose comes down a hair. A pilot who fights that and pulls back for altitude is a pilot about to stall.

Configuration changes are slow and deliberate. Flaps come down in steps at speeds the POH allows, which in Biscuit means the white arc, and the flap limit in her book is 85 knots. Flaps come up the same way. The handbook warns that raising them abruptly in slow flight can stall you, because you just took away part of the wing you were standing on.
How the exam asks it. Under ACS 6C, slow flight is flown without a stall warning. Know the plus 10, minus 0 airspeed tolerance and what pitch and power do behind the power curve.

A stall happens when the wing exceeds its critical angle of attack. Not a speed. An angle. You can stall at any airspeed and in any attitude, nose up, nose down, banked, if you ask the wing for more angle than it can give. The published stall speed is just the speed where that angle happens in one particular set of conditions. The handbook lists them: unaccelerated 1G flight, coordinated, at one weight, usually max gross, and at one CG, usually most forward. Change any of those and the number moves.

How you know it's coming. The horn. Mushy controls. A change in the sound of the air. Buffet, the shaking you feel through the yoke and the seat. And in a power-off stall, the handbook says the biggest cue may just be the yoke all the way back against the stop and the airplane coming down fast, because a power-off stall in a 172 is a polite, sinking thing. Power-on is sharper.

Recovery, every time, in this order. Reduce the angle of attack: push forward until the horn and the buffet quit. Roll the wings level. Add power. Then return to where you meant to be, climbing, with flaps coming up in steps. The order matters. The handbook calls out two classic errors by name: trying to level the wings before reducing the angle of attack, and trying to recover with power before reducing it. If a wing drops at the stall and you slam in opposite aileron, the down aileron on the low wing raises that wing's angle of attack, and you can make the stall on that side worse. Nose first. Then wings. Then power.

Power-off stalls simulate the approach to land. Landing configuration, power to idle, establish a normal descent, then raise the nose smoothly until it stalls. Practice some from a shallow turn, the base to final turn, and let it stall within about 90 degrees of heading change. Power-on stalls simulate takeoff and departure. Slow to liftoff speed, then add power, the ACS says no less than 65 percent, and pitch up until it breaks. The ACS keeps bank to 20 degrees or less, plus or minus 10, in turning stalls. On the checkride you recover promptly after a full stall. In the airplane with me, sometimes I'll ask for recovery at the first indication instead. The regulation wants you to know both.

Recover too hard, pull up too fast after a stall, and you can stall again. That's a secondary stall. It happens close to the ground because close to the ground is when you want the nose up most. And an accelerated stall is a stall at a higher than normal airspeed because the load factor is higher than 1G, in a steep turn or a hard pull. Which brings me to the math.
How the exam asks it. The first and most important action in any stall recovery is to reduce the angle of attack. An airplane can stall at any airspeed and attitude.

In a level turn, the wing has to hold the airplane up and pull it around the turn at the same time, so it makes more lift than the airplane weighs. The ratio is the load factor, in Gs. For a level, coordinated turn, load factor is 1 divided by the cosine of the bank angle. At 30 degrees, cosine is 0.866, so 1.15 Gs. At 45 degrees, cosine is 0.707, so 1.41. At 60 degrees, cosine is exactly 0.5, so 2.0. Twice your weight in the seat. At 60 degrees, Biscuit weighs 4,600 pounds as far as the wings are concerned.

Stall speed goes up with the square root of the load factor. So the stall speed in a turn is the 1G stall speed times the square root of n. Biscuit's POH lists a flaps-up stall at 50 knots calibrated at max weight, wings level. At 45 degrees, square root of 1.414 is 1.189, times 50, about 59. At 60 degrees, square root of 2 is 1.414, times 50, about 71. Her POH table says 59 and 71. Notice the curve. Going from level to 30 degrees costs you less than 4 knots. Going from 45 to 60 costs you 11. The handbook makes the same point: load factor climbs at a terrific rate past 45 or 50 degrees, and at 75 degrees a level turn is past the 3.8 G limit for a normal category airplane like ours.

Maneuvering speed, VA, is the speed below which a single full control deflection, or a gust, won't overstress the airplane. Below VA, the wing stalls before it breaks. Above it, you can break things before the wing quits. Here's the part people miss: VA goes down when the airplane is lighter. The PHAK example is 100 knots heavy and 90 knots light. Biscuit's POH gives 97 knots at 2,300 pounds, 89 at 1,950, and 80 at 1,600. A lighter airplane gets pushed around more by the same gust, so it needs a lower speed for the same protection. You solo light. Remember that.

And keep in mind that a lighter airplane stalls slower too, by the square root of the weight ratio. Same rule, other direction. Biscuit without me in her is about 150 pounds lighter, which means she'll climb better, float longer, and sit a couple of knots higher in the flare than you're used to. People get surprised by that on their first solo. You won't be, because I just told you.
How the exam asks it. Expect a load factor chart or a bank angle and a stall speed. Multiply the stall speed by the square root of the load factor. Know that VA decreases with weight.

A spin is a stall with yaw. That's all it takes. One wing more stalled than the other, the airplane yawing toward the more stalled wing, and it autorotates down in a corkscrew. Both ingredients have to be there. If you're coordinated at the stall, both wings stall about together and the nose just drops. If you're skidding or slipping at the stall, it can roll and go. The handbook says a stall in a slipping or skidding turn can spin in the direction of the rudder you're holding, regardless of which wingtip is up.

The four phases are entry, incipient, developed, and recovery. Incipient is the first two to four turns, when it's still settling into the spin. Developed is when the rotation, airspeed, and descent rate have all stabilized. The first turn loses about a thousand feet, and each turn after that about half as much. Do that math against our practice area. Enter at 7,700 over Bennett, lose a thousand in the first turn, and you're at 6,700, which is below 7,006. One turn and you've already gone through the floor. This is why we don't spin Biscuit, and why the ACS asks you to know spins and doesn't ask you to fly one. The skills section for spin awareness is literally left blank.

Recovery, from the handbook's template, when the POH doesn't say otherwise. The POH always wins. Power to idle, because power flattens a spin and speeds it up. Ailerons neutral. Full rudder opposite the rotation, briskly, and hold it. Then forward elevator, briskly, right after the rudder, without waiting for the rotation to stop. When the rotation stops, neutralize the rudder. Then ease out of the dive without pulling so hard you stall again. Some people use PARE to remember the first four: power, ailerons, rudder, elevator. Use the turn coordinator's little airplane to find the direction of rotation. The ball lies in a spin.

Where spins actually happen is at 600 feet on base to final. You overshoot the centerline because you had a tailwind on base. You don't want to steepen the bank, so you push a little inside rudder to bring the nose around. Now you're skidding. The bank creeps up, the nose drops, you pull back. That's every ingredient. The handbook's advice is plain. Low in the pattern, be reluctant to use more than 30 degrees of bank, never skid to fix an overshoot, and go around. Walt will tell you a story about this Wednesday. He'll want you to have read this first.

How the exam asks it. An airplane must be stalled to spin. Skidding turns near the ground are the classic setup. Recovery starts with power to idle, neutral ailerons, and full rudder opposite the rotation.

A steep turn on the checkride is a 360 degree turn at about 45 degrees of bank, then another the other way. The ACS standard: entry altitude plus or minus 100 feet, airspeed plus or minus 10 knots, bank plus or minus 5 degrees, and roll out on your entry heading within 10 degrees. Enter at the manufacturer's recommended speed, or if there isn't one, no faster than VA. Solo weight, Biscuit's VA is about 87. I use 85, dual or solo, so I don't have to remember which one I am.

Clear the area. Pick a far off reference on the horizon to roll out on, a grain elevator, the notch in the hills. Roll in smoothly and, before you pass about 30 degrees, start adding back pressure and some power, because the wing needs more angle to hold you up and more angle means more drag. Then hold it. Watch the nose and both wingtips against the horizon, not the gauges. The handbook says pilots who only watch the nose lose altitude. Somewhere past 30 degrees you'll feel the overbanking tendency, the airplane wanting to roll further on its own because the outside wing is moving faster. You hold a little opposite aileron against it.

The common failure is the nose sliding low, the altitude unwinding, and the pilot pulling harder to fix it. Don't. Pulling in a steep bank mostly tightens the turn and adds load, and the descent gets worse. The handbook's fix is in order: first shallow the bank with coordinated aileron and rudder, then raise the nose with back pressure, then go back to 45. Bank first. Then pitch.

Rollout. Start rolling out about half your bank angle before the heading. At 45 degrees, that's 22 or so degrees early. As you roll out, let off the back pressure and bring the power back, or you'll balloon up 150 feet and blow the altitude standard after a perfect turn. Which everybody does once.
How the exam asks it. Memorize the steep turn standards. If the nose drops in a steep turn, reduce the bank before adding back pressure.
Ground reference: flying a shape over the ground.

Ground reference maneuvers teach you to fly a path over the ground while the air underneath you is moving. They're the traffic pattern with the runway taken away. The ACS lists three, and the examiner picks at least one: the rectangular course, S-turns, and turns around a point. All three are flown 600 to 1,000 feet above the ground, altitude plus or minus 100 feet and airspeed plus or minus 10 knots.

The whole trick is one sentence: the faster your groundspeed, the steeper the bank you need to hold the same radius. Downwind, you're fast over the ground, so your bank is steepest. Upwind, you're slow, so it's shallowest. Crosswind, it's in between, and you're crabbed. You enter downwind, so the steepest bank comes first, when you're fresh and the point is clear. The handbook says don't go past 45 degrees. If the downwind bank is getting steep, you're too close. Leave and come back wider.

Rectangular course: pick a field, fly a box around it a half to three quarters of a mile outside the edges, and enter at 45 degrees to the downwind side, just like the pattern. That's the point. The turn from downwind to base is the steepest one, and if you don't steepen it you'll get blown wide, which is exactly how people overshoot final at the airport. S-turns: pick a straight road perpendicular to the wind, cross it at 90 degrees heading downwind, fly a half circle, cross it again with the wings level right over the road, and do the other half the other way. Turns around a point: pick something small and visible, enter downwind at the radius you want, and keep it at the same distance all the way around by changing the bank continuously.

In a high wing airplane, the low wing hides your point in a left turn from the left seat. Pick your altitude and radius so you can see it, or ask me to give you right turns. And pick a point that isn't somebody's house. Center pivot irrigation hubs out east are perfect. They're small, they're in the middle of an empty field, and nobody's going to call the airport about you.
How the exam asks it. The classic question: where in a turn around a point is the bank steepest? Where the groundspeed is highest, heading downwind.

Three red marks. Question four: Student pilot. Minimum flight visibility, day, for a solo. She'd written 1 SM, thinking of Class G. Question nine: Biscuit's max flap extended speed. She'd written 110, which was the number for ten degrees only, and Abby had underlined the word ONLY in the question that Jordan had read right past. Question twenty six: Once you're signed off to solo, where may you land? She'd written ANY AIRPORT WITHIN 25 NM, which Abby had circled and written next to it, in green, who told you that.
Nobody had. She'd made it up from half a sentence in a book and believed it.
Abby leaned back. The rule says I review every one you got wrong before I let you go. How do you want to do it?
A. Ask Abby to just tell her the three right answers so they can get to the flying part faster.
B. Take the test home, look up all three tonight, and text Abby what she finds before Tuesday.
C. One at a time: say why she picked it, find the source, and write the right answer in her own words.
D. Point out that 27 of 30 is 90 percent, well over the 70 the FAA test needs, and move on.

She does all three the way she'd do a missed med on a QA review: what she thought, where she got it, what the rule actually says. 61.89(a)(6), 3 SM by day. The flap page, with ONLY in bold in the POH too. 61.93(a), and the two sentences that say a solo student lands where she left unless she's been trained and endorsed for somewhere else. She writes each one on an index card. Abby watches her write the third card and doesn't say anything. Then she says, Twenty six is the one I'd have lost sleep over. A student who thinks she can land anywhere is a student who lands somewhere.

That's it. 61.87(b)(2) requires the instructor to review all incorrect answers before authorizing solo. Working out why you missed each one, and finding the source, fixes the reasoning instead of the answer. A student solo lands only at the airport of origin unless endorsed under 61.93.
Decision two. What goes in the pocket.

Monday night she laid it out on the kitchen counter the way she checked the rig at the start of a shift. The plastic student pilot certificate that had come in the mail in May, white and blue, with a photo of her that looked like a hostage. The third class medical from April. Her driver's license. Her logbook, thirty eight hours, most of it in green. And the composition notebook, which wasn't any kind of document but sat on the counter with the rest of it because that's where it lived now.
A text from Abby Strand. Homework. What do you legally need with you on a local solo. And what do you bring anyway. Short answer.
A. Certificate, medical, and photo ID are required. The logbook isn't, on a local solo, but it comes.
B. Just the logbook. The endorsement is what makes the solo legal, and the plastic cards can stay home.
C. The logbook and her license. The plastic student card is only for the checkride, so it stays home.
D. Certificate, medical, ID, and logbook. All four are required by regulation on every solo flight.

She types it, with the section numbers, because she's her. 61.3 for the certificate and the ID, the medical with them. 61.51 for the logbook on cross-countries only. Logbook comes anyway. So does the endorsement page, flagged. Abby: correct. Also correct that you flagged it. Ramp checks happen. Then, a minute later: what did you bring that isn't on the list. Jordan looks at the green notebook. She doesn't answer that one.

Yep. That's the one. 61.3(a) requires the pilot certificate and a photo ID in the pilot's possession or readily accessible in the aircraft, and the medical certificate has to be with them too. 61.51(i)(2) requires the logbook and student certificate on solo cross-countries. On a local solo the logbook isn't required, but it holds the endorsements, so carry it.
Decision three. I won't even count.
Tuesday night, 8:15, FaceTime, and Ellie's face was too close to the camera, so it was mostly one eye and a freckle. Claire had told her. Claire told her things now. That was new.
Mom says you're going to fly Biscuit by yourself. The eye backed up and became a whole face. When you do it, can I sit in the back? I'll be so quiet. I won't even count the landings out loud.
Behind her, out of focus, Claire was doing the dishes and very carefully not looking at the phone.
A. "No, because it's too dangerous the first time. Something could go wrong and you'd be scared."
B. "Not till I'm a real pilot, El. Students can't take anybody. When I can, you're the first one."
C. "Maybe. Let me check with Abby whether there's any way to do it on the first one."
D. "Sure, El, if Abby says it's okay. I'll ask her tomorrow and see what she thinks."

Ellie chews on the inside of her cheek, which is how she thinks about everything, and wants to know if that's a rule or a Jordan rule. A real rule, Jordan tells her. The government kind. Okay. Then can I watch? Behind her the water's gone off. It's a school day, baby. Then take a picture. Jordan says she will, and after they hang up she writes PICTURE on her hand in blue Bic. Danny used to do that. She never had, until tonight.

Exactly right. A student pilot may not carry passengers under 61.89(a)(1). Saying so plainly, with the reason, is honest and doesn't leave a promise that has to be broken. The privilege to carry passengers comes with the private certificate.
Decision four. Six hundred fifteen feet.

Tuesday, October 13, 7:20 in the morning, clear and cold, 2°C on the ground and the plains east of the airport gone the color of a paper bag. Bennett went by off the left wing, a water tower and a grain elevator and the interstate drawn straight through the middle of it with a ruler. Biscuit was at 6,900 and climbing, slowly, because it was the end of a long climb.
Slow flight first, then stalls. Pick your altitude and tell me why.
Jordan had done the math on the drive, at a red light on Arapahoe, and written it on the kneeboard under SHELF AT 80.
A. 7,400 over the field. That's 1,515 feet above it, so it meets the floor exactly.
B. 8,500, with a call to Denver Approach, since there's so little room under the shelf out here.
C. 7,700 over Bennett. Ground is about 5,500, so the floor is 7,000, and she's under the shelf.
D. 7,000 over the field. That's eleven hundred above the ground and a thousand under the shelf.

Say the floor. Seven thousand six, call it seven. Shelf at eight. Entering at seventy seven hundred. Abby nods at the altimeter, then out the window at the grain elevator. Over the field you'd have six hundred feet to work with. Out here, a thousand. That's why the practice area is out here. It's not the scenery. Clearing turns, left and right, wing up to look above. A Cherokee way off south, low, going away. Nobody else.

That's it. The ACS requires slow flight and stalls to be completed no lower than 1,500 ft AGL. Over Bennett at about 5,500 ft that's about 7,000 MSL, and the Class B floor is 8,000. Entering at 7,700 leaves room for altitude loss above the floor while staying clear of the shelf.

Full flaps, 7,700, heading 090 toward a grain elevator, airspeed 50 and power at about 1,900 on the tach, which meant 1,850. The nose was high enough that Jordan had to look out the side to see the horizon. The yoke felt like it was attached to the airplane by rubber bands. Her right foot was doing more than she'd told it to.

A little bump came through, the kind you'd never notice at cruise, and the stall horn went off. A short, sour chirp from the left wing root, like a kazoo with a grudge. Then again. The altimeter was ticking down, 7,680, 7,670.
Abby had her hands folded. ACS says no horn. A bump's forgivable if you fix it. Fix it.
A. Ease the nose down a hair to quiet the horn, then add a little power to hold the altitude.
B. Add full power and climb until the horn quits for good, then come back down to 7,700.
C. Raise the flaps to 10 degrees, so the wing has more margin above the stall at this airspeed.
D. Pull back a little to stop the altitude loss. The horn is normal this slow, so let it chirp.

Nose down, a degree, maybe less. The horn stops in the middle of a chirp. The altimeter keeps sliding, so she brings the throttle up a hundred RPM, and it stops at 7,660 and comes back, slowly, to 7,700. Fifty three knots. She keeps it there. Right rudder, a little more. A turn to the left, 20 degrees, more power, and the horn doesn't make a sound. There. That's your number for full flaps. Fifty three. Pitch for the speed, power for the altitude. Upside down from everything you've done so far. Welcome to slow flight.

Yep. That's the one. AFH: in slow flight, react to any stall warning by reducing angle of attack slightly, then add power to maintain altitude. Below L/D max, pitch controls airspeed and power controls altitude. The ACS wants no stall warning and airspeed plus 10, minus 0.

Power-off stall. Carb heat on, power back, flaps down in steps, a stabilized descent at 65 like final approach. Throttle to idle. Then, smoothly, back on the yoke, and keep coming, and the nose rose until all she could see was sky and the horn was steady and the yoke was all the way back in her lap.

The buffet came up through her seat. Then Biscuit quit, the nose dropping, and in the same instant the left wing fell away, fifteen degrees, twenty, the horizon tilting in the windshield like a picture on a wall that somebody had bumped.
Every instinct she had was in her right hand.
A. Right aileron, hard, to pick the left wing up before it rolls any further, then lower the nose.
B. Full power first, so she doesn't lose any more altitude, then lower the nose and level the wings.
C. Lower the nose, level the wings, add power, then pull up quickly to save every foot she can.
D. Forward on the yoke until the buffet quits, then roll the wings level, then add full power.

Forward. Not a shove, a firm push, and the horn cuts off and the buffet goes with it, and the wings are flying again. Then she rolls level, coordinated, a lot of right rudder. Then full throttle, carb heat off, and Biscuit's nose wants to come up on its own, so she holds it at a climb attitude. Flaps 20. Climbing, barely. Flaps 10. Flaps up. 7,520 on the altimeter, so a hundred eighty feet gone. Nose. Wings. Power. You did it in order, which is all I care about.

Exactly right. The AFH stall recovery: reduce angle of attack until the stall warning is eliminated, roll the wings level with coordinated controls, add power, then return to the desired flightpath with flaps retracted in increments. Reducing AOA is the most important step.

The October safety meeting was Wednesday at seven in Hangar Six, nine folding chairs and seven people, including Russ on Marisol's phone propped against a quart of oil. Walt stood at the whiteboard next to Danny's capitals and Marisol's, with a dry erase marker he kept capping and uncapping.

He drew a runway. Then a base leg, and an arrow on it for the wind, from behind. I read a report like this once. Doesn't matter where. Pilot with four hundred hours, nice day, tailwind on base they didn't notice. Turned final late, went through the centerline, and didn't want to steepen the bank, because everybody says don't bank steep low. So they fixed it with their feet. He drew the airplane's path curling past the runway and stopped the line in the grass. Six hundred feet. That's where it ends.
He looked at the chairs. Then at her. Jordan. You're on base, you've overshot, the runway's sliding off to your left. What do you do.
A. A little inside rudder to bring the nose around without steepening the bank any further.
B. Hold a shallow bank, 30 degrees at most, and if that won't line her up, go around and try again.
C. Fly through the centerline, then S-turn back onto final from the other side of the runway.
D. Steepen to 45 degrees, coordinated, and tighten the turn. Steep turns are for exactly this.

Walt looks at her for a while. Then he writes GO AROUND on the board, under the runway, in capitals that look a little like Danny's. Free. Every time. Costs you four minutes and your pride, and you have more of both than you think. Afterward, folding chairs, he passes her on the way to the door. Abby says Saturday. It isn't a question. I'll be at the fence.

That's it. The AFH: at the low altitude of a base to final turn, be reluctant to use more than 30 degrees of bank and never skid to fix an overshoot. The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around.

Back on Tuesday, after the stalls, the steep turns. 85 knots, 7,700, heading 360 toward a white grain elevator on the horizon that she'd decided was hers. Clearing turns. Roll left. At 30 degrees she started the back pressure and added a hundred RPM, and at 45 she held it, the horizon lying across the windshield at a slant and the left wingtip pinned on a section line road far below.

Then she got interested in the wingtip. The bank crept to 50. The nose slid down below where it lived. The airspeed was 90, then 93, and the altimeter was unwinding, 7,650, 7,620, the VSI needle pointing at the floor.
A. Roll back to about 40 first, then add back pressure to raise the nose, then 45 again.
B. Pull back firmly to stop the descent while holding the bank right where it is now.
C. Roll out to wings level, climb back to 7,700, and start the whole turn over from the top.
D. Add full power to climb back up to 7,700 while keeping the bank at about 50 degrees.

A little right aileron and rudder, back to 40. Then the nose comes up easily, like it's been waiting for permission. 7,620, 7,660, 7,690. Back to 45, a hair of left aileron against the overbanking. She picks the grain elevator up over the nose, 22 degrees early, and rolls out, letting the back pressure off as she goes, and the needle stays on 7,700. Heading 002. Eighty low and eight fast at the worst. Inside the standard, barely. Now the other way, and watch the wings, not the road.

Yep. That's the one. AFH steep turns: correct a nose low altitude loss by first reducing bank with coordinated aileron and rudder, then increasing pitch with back pressure. Roll out about half the bank angle before the heading. ACS: altitude ±100 ft, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5°, heading ±10°.

Wednesday, October 14, 7:40. A second short flight, ground reference work, 6,300 feet over a wheat stubble field south of Bennett. Eight hundred feet above the ground, which felt like flying through somebody's living room after a week at 7,700.

The wind at altitude was out of the west, 270 at 15, Abby said, and you could see it in the dust from a farm truck on a dirt road, a tan plume going east like a flag. Out in the middle of the stubble sat the hub of a center pivot sprinkler, a little steel tower in the middle of a huge circle. Nothing near it. Not a house for half a mile. No cows either, and Jordan checked twice, because the handbook had been weirdly firm about cows.
Pivot. Right turns, so the wing doesn't eat it. Where do you come in, and where's the bank steepest?
A. Hold a steady 30 degree bank all the way around and see where the wind takes the circle.
B. Enter heading downwind, steepest bank there, then shallowest when she's flying into the wind.
C. Enter heading into the wind, so the slow groundspeed gives her time to set up the bank.
D. Enter downwind with a moderate bank, then correct the radius wherever she sees the pivot drift.

She comes in from the west, heading east with the wind behind her, a quarter mile north of the hub, and rolls right, fast, to 40 degrees, because the ground's going by at a hundred knots and that's no time to be shy. Coming around through south, then west, the ground slows down and she lets the bank off. 40. 30. About 15 when she's pointed straight into the wind and the hub's barely creeping by. Then she builds it back. The truck's dust shows her where she's drifting. Two laps. On the second one the hub sits pinned just off the wing strut like somebody bolted it there. That's the traffic pattern, Abby says, pleased with the hub, or with Jordan, hard to tell. Every base turn you'll ever make. Now you know why some days you overshoot.

Exactly right. AFH: enter ground reference maneuvers downwind, where groundspeed is highest and the steepest bank is needed. Bank decreases as groundspeed decreases toward the upwind position, then increases again. No more than about 45 degrees.
Abby signed nothing Wednesday. She said Saturday at ten, after Jordan's shift. Thursday to Friday, you sleep Friday, Saturday you're mine.

Twenty four on, forty eight off, and she'd traded a shift that week so Saturday came out clear. Then Friday at six in the morning, an hour before she got off, the captain asked who could stay over. Two people out sick. Jordan said yes because she always said yes. Forty eight hours at the station, maybe twelve of them asleep, in pieces.

At 4:10 Saturday morning they worked a cardiac arrest on a kitchen floor off Colfax, a man in his fifties with his wife holding the dog in the doorway, and they got him back. Pulse on the third check. He was talking, sort of, by the time they rolled into the ER. It was a good one. It was the kind you get maybe twice a year. She was shaking a little in the ambulance bay afterward and told herself it was the cold.

7:25 AM, the station parking lot. Thirty six hours awake, give or take. Her hands felt fine. Her head felt like a bright room with the lights on too long. The sky over the plains was perfect, clear to Kansas, no wind. Of course.
A text from Abby Strand. ATIS says calm and clear. I'm at the field at 9:30. Bring a shirt you don't love.
A. Go to the airport anyway and let Abby decide after she gets a look at her in person.
B. Nap in the car until nine, drink a big coffee, and go. Two hours of sleep is enough for three laps.
C. Fly. She's worked tired a hundred times, and this is three laps around the pattern, not Moab.
D. Text Abby the truth, push the solo to another day, and drive home and sleep.

She types it with her thumbs in the cold: Held over. Worked a code at 4. Been up 36 hrs. I'm not flying today. Then she sits there and stares at it before she sends it, because sending it makes it real, and Saturday was going to be the day. She sends it. Abby answers in under a minute: Good. That's the best decision you've made since I met you. Tuesday 7am, sleep Monday. Then: did the code make it. Jordan writes yes. Abby writes good again, and that's it. She drives home with the window down so she stays awake and sleeps until four in the afternoon.

That's it. IMSAFE: Fatigue. After 36 hours awake, judgment and reaction time are impaired whether or not you feel it. Pushing a first solo costs a few days. Flying it impaired removes the safety margin on the one flight where no one else is aboard.
Tuesday, October 20. She'd slept nine hours. The ATIS at 7:20 said wind three four zero at six, ten miles, sky clear, temperature three, altimeter three zero one four. Under every number on the card.

7:30. Abby flew three laps with her, stop and goes, and said nothing on any of them except Mm. 7:52. They taxied back to the ramp. Abby got the logbook out, wrote for a long time on her knee, and then turned around in her seat to look at Jordan.

I told you I'd get out at the runup. Ground says no pedestrians on Alpha, so I'm getting out here. Three, full stop. I'll be on the handheld. Jordan pulled the mixture; Abby climbed out behind the strut and shut the right door from outside. Right one does it too, if you shut it from outside. Check mine. She headed for the fence where Walt already was, and Marisol, and the empty seat sat there next to Jordan like a person. Jordan started Biscuit again.

7:56. Centennial Ground, Cessna Niner One Echo, student pilot, west ramp, taxi for departure. Ground cleared her to 35R via Alpha, and she taxied it alone, which felt like driving a car with nobody in the passenger seat for the first time at sixteen. 7:58. Runup, in the runup area on Alpha near the end of 35R. Mags, carb heat, mixture, the top latch of her own door, twice, out loud. She told ground she was ready for departure, and ground told her to hold short of 35R and monitor tower. Solid lines in front of her, nose short of them. 8:03. Cessna Niner One Echo, runway three five right, cleared for takeoff. 8:04. Full throttle. Airspeed alive. Fifty five. She eased back, and Biscuit, a hundred and fifty pounds lighter than she'd ever felt her, came off the runway like she'd been let off a leash, and there was a bang on the right side like a shotgun.

The right door was open. Three inches, then six, then back to three, flapping on the slipstream with a roar that filled the whole cabin. The checklist on the right seat went out the gap and was gone. Nobody had latched the top of the right door. Abby always did hers.
A. Turn left right away and land on 35L, the parallel, so the door doesn't come off.
B. Pull the power and put it back down on the runway now, while there's still runway ahead of her.
C. Leave it. Fly the airplane, climb out, fly a normal pattern, and land. Close it on the ground.
D. Unbuckle, lean across the right seat, and pull the door shut while the airplane climbs out.

Fly the airplane. She says it out loud, which nobody can hear but her. Pitch for VY. Right rudder. The door bangs, settles, bangs. Seven hundred feet a minute up, more than she's ever seen, because there's nobody in the right seat. She levels at 6,900 on the crosswind leg long before she's used to, and the roar is just a noise now. Centennial Tower, Niner One Echo, my right door came open on takeoff. No problem, I'd like a full stop. Niner One Echo, roger, make right traffic, runway three five right, cleared to land. Downwind. Carb heat. Flaps. A normal approach, a normal landing, the door sighing shut on its own when she slows below forty. On the taxiway, stopped, past the lines, she reaches over and latches it. Top and bottom. Then she checks it again.

Yep. That's the one. AFH door opening in flight: concentrate on flying the airplane. If the door opens after liftoff, don't rush to land: climb to pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern, and land normally. Leave the door alone and close it once safely on the ground.

8:14. Second takeoff, door latched, both latches, she'd touched them like a rosary. Climbing out she noticed that she was talking. Out loud, steadily, the whole time, the way she talked a patient through a line placement. Okay. VY. Right rudder. Shelf at eight. Look left. Crosswind turn. Nobody to hear it but Biscuit.

8:19. Base, final. Same power as always, same flaps, and Biscuit wouldn't come down. Without Abby in her she floated on the descent like a paper airplane. At five hundred feet Jordan was a little high and she let it go. At three hundred feet the PAPI was four white, the airspeed was 75 instead of 65, and the aiming point blocks were going to go by underneath her.
Ten thousand feet of runway in front of her. Plenty of room. That was the thing about having plenty of room.
A. Push the nose down at the numbers and get it on the runway now, while there's runway left to stop.
B. Hold it off and float it down the runway until it settles on its own. It'll touch down eventually.
C. Slip it down to the PAPI, then land a bit long. There's ten thousand feet of runway to do it.
D. Go around. Full power, carb heat off, right rudder, climb, flaps up in steps, and fly the lap again.

Throttle in. Carb heat off. Right rudder for the nose, which wants to climb the wall. Flaps 20, 10, up. Niner One Echo, going around. Niner One Echo, roger, make right traffic. Nobody tells her it was right. She knows. Downwind again, and this time she pulls a little more power abeam the numbers, because Biscuit is lighter and she's going to need less, and on final the PAPI is two and two. Over at the fence, somebody's hand comes out of a pocket. She doesn't look long enough to count.

Exactly right. AFH: if the approach isn't stabilized by 500 ft, go around, and if it comes apart below 300 ft, go around immediately. A go-around is power, attitude, configuration: full power with carb heat off, pitch to climb, flaps up in increments.

8:31. Third takeoff. Both latches. On the climbout the low sun came across the plains off the right wing, and the whole east side of the airport went gold for a minute, the hangar roofs and the fuel truck and the grass between the runways. She didn't look long. She looked.

8:34. Downwind, 6,900, ninety knots. She was still talking. She'd stopped hearing herself do it somewhere on the second lap, the way you stop hearing a monitor until it changes pitch. Abeam the numbers. Carb heat. Fifteen hundred. Ten degrees. And then, without planning to, Okay, Danny, and she heard that one, and kept flying.

8:37. Final. Two white, two red. Sixty five knots, and she took a couple more off this time, because the airplane was light, and the numbers came up and went under the nose and she held it, and held it, and the stall horn chirped once, the good kind, and the mains touched. Then the nose. Centerline under her, the white dashes going by slower and slower.
Cessna Niner One Echo, turn right at Alpha seven, contact ground. A pause on the frequency that didn't need to be there. Nice job on the first solo.
Right at Alpha seven, over to ground, Niner One Echo. She almost said thank you, and then said it. Thank you. All the way past the hold lines. Tail too.
At the fence, Walt's hand was up. She was close enough, rolling by on Alpha, to count. Eight fingers. He held them there until she was past, and put them away.

8:46. Mixture cutoff. Mags off. Master off. The quiet came in all at once, like it always did, and for a second she just sat there with her hands on her knees and the headset still on, Danny's headset, which Marisol had handed her that morning at 6:50 without a word, in the padded bag that had been sitting in the bottom of her toolbox since March.

It was gray, older than the club loaner and heavier, with the left ear seal cracked and fixed with black tape. On the headband, scratched into the plastic with something sharp, D.R. Clipped to the cord was a clothespin, to keep it from swinging into the throttle, and Marisol had said only, He'd want it flying. I'm done keeping it in a drawer. Then she'd gone back to her bench and started safety wiring something that didn't need it.
It fit. That was the stupid part. Jordan had braced for it not to fit.
Abby was at the wing strut before the prop stopped, with Marisol's big orange shears in her hand and her face doing something it didn't usually do. Out. Turn around.

Jordan climbed out and turned around. She'd worn her oldest station T-shirt, the one from the B shift chili cookoff, with a bleach spot shaped like Ohio. Abby pulled the back of it out of her jeans and cut. One long crooked cut across the tail, all the way, and then she held it up, a ragged navy rectangle with half of CHILI on it, and wrote on it in Sharpie on Biscuit's cowling, in block capitals: JORDAN REYES. FIRST SOLO. N4791E. KAPA. 10/20/26. Then, smaller: 3 T/O, 3 FULL STOP, 1 DOOR.
You flew it like somebody who's been scared on purpose before, Abby said, capping the pen. Which is the whole job. That go-around was the best thing you did all morning.

Jordan's logbook, endorsements. 10/12/26. I certify that Jordan E. Reyes has satisfactorily completed the pre-solo knowledge test of 14 CFR 61.87(b) for the Cessna 172N aircraft.. /s/ 10/12/26 A. Strand 3418862CFI RE 06-30-2027. 10/20/26. I certify that Jordan E. Reyes has received and logged pre-solo flight training for the maneuvers and procedures that are appropriate to the Cessna 172N aircraft. I have determined they have demonstrated satisfactory proficiency and safety on the maneuvers and procedures required by 14 CFR 61.87 in this or similar make and model of aircraft to be flown.. /s/ 10/20/26 A. Strand 3418862CFI RE 06-30-2027. 10/20/26. I certify that Jordan E. Reyes has received the required training to qualify for solo flying. I have determined they meet the applicable requirements of 14 CFR 61.87(n) and are proficient to make solo flights in Cessna 172N.. Limitations: Day VFR only. KAPA traffic pattern only until further endorsed. Surface wind 10 knots or less, gusts no more than 5 over, crosswind component 5 knots or less. Ceiling 3,000 AGL or higher, visibility 5 SM or better. No passengers (14 CFR 61.89). Latch both doors.. /s/ 10/20/26 A. Strand 3418862CFI RE 06-30-2027. (green ink, and the last line added in a different pen, in the hangar)

In the hangar, Marisol had already cleared a spot on the corkboard by the door, under the old whiteboard with Danny's capitals and her own. A dozen shirt tails were pinned up there from twenty years of club members, gone pale under the shop lights. Marisol pushed in four pins, one at each corner, and stepped back and looked at it for a while with her arms crossed. Then she went back to her bench without saying anything, and a minute later she was singing along to the radio, badly, which Jordan had learned was the same thing.

Walt came in from the fence with his collar up. He didn't look at the shirt tail. He looked at Jordan. Eight, he said. In case you didn't count. Then he picked up the logbook off Marisol's bench, read the endorsement page with his glasses on the end of his nose, initialed the monthly box on the inside cover, and put it down. I don't give tens.
He stopped. Looked at her over the glasses. Then he laughed, once, short, like something had gotten out before he could stop it, and walked out to his truck.

When the hangar was quiet, she took the green notebook out of her flight bag and sat on the step of Marisol's stepladder with it. She'd been reading it in order again since August, mostly. In April she had flipped through the first pages and seen one with SOLO across the top in letters an inch tall, and turned past it fast, and put a paper clip on it, and hadn't looked since. She'd been saving it. She hadn't told herself that was what she was doing. She opened it at the clip.

Danny's logbook, a page from May, eleven years ago. May 9. SOLO!!! KAPA, C152 from the school, 0.6, 3 T/O, 3 full stop. Instructor got out at the runup, said "three, then come get me," and walked off like it was nothing. It was NOT nothing. Talked to myself the whole time. Tower heard some of it. Apparently I keyed the mic on downwind and said "okay Danny you beautiful idiot, carb heat," and the tower lady said "carb heat approved, Five Two Bravo." Landing 1: good. Landing 2: bounced, went around, didn't die. Landing 3: good enough. Instructor cut my shirt (the Broncos one, RIP). Called Mom from the airplane before I even got out. She yelled at me for using a phone in an airplane. Then she cried. Then she asked if I was eating enough. Don't tell her I wrote that. Lesson: the airplane is way lighter with nobody in the other seat. Nobody tells you that. Somebody should tell you that.
She read it twice. The second time she laughed out loud in the empty hangar, one bark, and Marisol looked up from her bench and then decided not to.

Somebody should tell you that. Abby had. Three times. She thought about Danny on downwind eleven years ago with the mic keyed, being heard, and herself this morning on the same downwind, talking the whole way, and nobody hearing any of it but Biscuit. Same habit, different airplane, different button. She found, sitting there on Marisol's stepladder, that she liked that. She'd expected to feel like she'd done something he had done. She felt like she'd done something, and he'd done it too.
It had been a clean two weeks, start to finish, and she could feel it in the way she'd put the notebook down, gently, like it was something that could be handed back.
She called her mother from the car.

Five rings, then voicemail. The recording was old, from when her mother still talked slower, and it said her full name, Lourdes Reyes, like she was checking in at a clinic. Jordan didn't leave a message. She put the phone face down on her leg, heater going, and looked out at Biscuit in her spot. Right door shut. She could see the top latch from here. Or thought she could. While she waited she ran the shutdown again in her head, since that's what her head did: mixture cutoff, mags off, master off, key on the dash, Hobbs written down, tie downs, gust lock.
Four minutes later the phone buzzed on her leg.

Mija. Her mother was breathing like she'd taken the stairs two at a time. Claire said it was today. I saw your name and I couldn't. I thought if I didn't pick up, then you were still up there and you were fine, and if I picked up it would be somebody else's voice. A long, long pause. Are you on the ground?
She was on the ground, Jordan told her. In the car. Parked.
Okay. She heard her mother sit down. The kitchen chair that scraped. Your brother called me from inside the airplane. I yelled at him.
Jordan said she knew. He'd written it down.

Nothing on the line for a while. Then a sound that could've been a laugh, or the other thing. Of course he did. Another long pause, the refrigerator humming in it. Jordan watched a fuel truck crawl by on the ramp, amber light, beeper, the driver eating a burrito with one hand and steering with the other. I'm still not getting in that airplane.
Next time, you call me before. So I can worry on time. Then, quiet enough that Jordan had to press the phone flat to her ear: Tell me how it was.

So she did, in order, like giving report at the ER doors: door open on rotation, three inches, then six, the noise, pattern, land, the latch. Then the hangar roofs going gold, the tower lady, Walt's eight fingers. Her mother didn't interrupt. At the door part she said Ay. Jordan kept going. When she got to the shirt tail her mother wanted to know which shirt, exactly. The one with the bleach on it? Good. That one was ugly.
